title: She grew up in group homes. Now she’s piecing together her past
summary: Marisa Wright, 37, is trying to piece together her broken childhood through school, police and government records. Some agencies initially supplied only a limited amount of information in a few…

image.caption: Marisa Wright, 37, accessed her personal records earlier this year. She was in provincial care from the age of 12 to 15. (Dave Irish/CBC)

blocks.text: WARNING: Details in this story discuss thoughts of suicide.
When Marisa Wright opened a thick paper file earlier this year detailing her childhood in government care, she thought she was ready.
Then she found a suicide note she'd written at the age of 15.

Typed in bold italic letters, Wright addressed the goodbye message to her friends and family saying she wanted to be “out of this world.” She recalls writing it on a school computer in Truro, isolated from her classmates.
“Honestly, I just wanted to die,” said Wright. “I felt so unloved.”
More than two decades later, she was shocked to see the note had been stored in her personal records for all of that time.
“I see a girl that was broken that really needed help. And nobody gave her help. Literally crying out on a page,” she said.
Why this woman fought to learn about a childhood spent in group homes

Wright, 37, is trying to decipher the holes of her childhood through school, police and government records. As an adult, she has faced a series of traumatic events that left her questioning how she became so fragile.

“I'm piecing everything together and seeing all the areas and all the times that I really needed help, and nobody gave it to me. So now I'm giving myself that help that I needed back then, and I'm building myself up,” said Wright.

Some agencies initially supplied only limited information in a few summary pages and others denied access completely — a common response, according to one expert who says former youth in care have a right to full, unredacted files and mental health support.

“It can be very traumatic to see how you were talked about in your case files from the various social workers that were in your life,” said Melanie Doucet, adjunct professor at the McGill University School of Social Work and project lead of the National Council of Youth in Care Advocates.
Melanie Doucet, a McGill University adjunct professor and former youth in care, says people deserve access to their full records with mental health support. (Submitted by Melanie Doucet)

As a former child in care in New Brunswick, Doucet understands how triggering it can be for people with a history of complex trauma to receive information about their childhood. She says that’s why she has been pushing for better access to therapy for youth currently and formerly in government care.
“This is a lifelong healing process for a lot of young people who've been through the system and it needs to be offered as soon as they enter into the system, not after they're adults,” said Doucet.

Robert Wright, president of the Nova Scotia College of Social Workers and founder of the Peoples' Counselling Clinic in Halifax, believes at the very least anyone receiving their personal file should have a clinician present when they open it for the first time.
“We recognize that reviewing a history, even though you were there, reviewing the history is traumatic,” he said.
“People need to — when they’re unpacking their history, whether that’s their history of sexual violence, their history of abuse, or their history of being in care — they need very real support.”
Marisa Wright's file was released through the province's disclosure program in February after a one-year wait. (CBC)

For Marisa Wright, seeing her own file validated memories from her childhood that were often brushed away. But then, feelings of despair and anger bubbled to the surface and quickly became overwhelming.

While she has sought counselling support in recent years, funding for sessions has been limited through non-profit programs. She says she does not have the means to access private therapy and wishes more free services were available.

In a written statement, the Department of Opportunities and Social Development said when people access their files through its disclosure program, a social worker is assigned to “assist people through the process of requesting, receiving and learning about their history.”
Wright said that support wasn’t made clear to her.

“I don’t think that the unit that provides information to people about their history of child welfare is sufficiently staffed to provide the necessary clinical support to the people who are inquiring,” said Robert Wright.
According to documents obtained through a freedom of information request, the disclosure program has eight provincial staff members including six social workers.

Marisa Wright received her personal file through the disclosure program in February. There were details she wasn't expecting in the stack of documents, while other details were not included at all. (Dave Irish/CBC)

In the weeks after she received her file last February, Marisa Wright wrestled again with thoughts of giving up. Then she started writing poems and posting videos on social media, which she says eased the burden inside her head.
“The more that I write, the more that I put this out, the more that I read … it's all coming back to me, and I feel like I deserve a place in this world,” said Wright.
“I deserve answers.”
Broken childhood

From the age of 12, Wright bounced between group homes and schools throughout Nova Scotia until she was discharged from provincial care at the age of 15 — the same year she typed the suicide note in school.

She says her life completely unravelled following a sexual assault in 2004 that happened while she was "gone without permission" from a group home in rural Pictou County. A provincial document in her personal file outlines how police questioned the credibility of Wright’s allegations and did not proceed with charges. Staff members at the home noticed she became anxious and angry, according to the documents.

Then, following a weekend visit with her family soon after the incident, Wright refused to return because she didn’t feel safe. Her bed was held for one month as she struggled with whether to come back, according to an unsigned release letter included in her file.
“Historically, Marisa was noted to be a runner and although for the most part she physically stopped this behaviour she proceeded to emotionally run from her issues,” the letter stated.
Marisa Wright spent her early teen years bouncing between schools and group homes in Nova Scotia. (Marisa Wright/Submitted)

Her file consistently paints her as a child who tended to bully her peers and lash out — points Wright doesn’t deny. However, she maintains no one ever asked why she was acting out, or what happened before she ended up in government care.
To this day, Wright doesn’t understand how provincial staff members allowed her to return to an unstable home environment.
“I just remember my house being a crack house. It was the party spot where people would come to get messed up, and a lot of bad things happened,” she said.
“The province had a duty to protect me, and they didn't.”
In a written statement, the department told CBC it was unable to comment on individual cases but “a care and custody order would be a determination made by the courts.”
Expert says Wright’s experience is widespread
Doucet said this is, sadly, a common story across the country. But she believes Wright’s account should be a wake-up call for officials in charge of youth in care.
“Dismissing cries for help like that is what results in deaths in the system,” said Doucet.
“We have to be going to the root causes of things if we want to truly make a difference in the lives of young people and have things resolved so that they have a chance to have a successful future.”
Wright also believes change within the system is possible. She continues to recite poems and share her lived experience on social media, which she says has resulted in a surprising response.
“The amount of people that commented and encouraged me and said, you know, this is amazing. And we see you, we hear you and we believe you,” Wright said.
“I've always wanted to help people, and I feel like if I put my stuff out there, my story, that I can resonate with other people.”

They are among society's most vulnerable: children who experience traumatic instability and end up in government care. In this series called “Left Behind,” the CBC Atlantic investigative team explores the challenges and outcomes through the eyes of people who lived through this and those trying to help them.
